Subject: TTFT & streaming requirements — follow-up and proposed SLOs

Hi Alyssa / Tom —

Thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we have everything on the same page:

Summary of your requirements (as I heard them):
- Time-to-first-token (TTFT): target <= 150ms p95 for short prompts (<= 512 tokens) for chat assistant flows.
- Streaming: SSE or WebSocket preferred for real-time UX; chunk cadence should be ~50-100ms between chunks for a smooth progressive render.
- Throughput/concurrency: expected steady-state ~80 RPS with spikes to 300 RPS for peak windows (5-10 minute bursts).
- Concurrency per session: up to 8 concurrent streams per user in your most active workflows.
- Availability: SLA target discussed: 99.9% for inference endpoints, with fallbacks to lower-cost variants during sustained regional capacity pressure.

Questions we had for your engineering team:
1) Are the TTFT targets uniform across all models, or only for primary chat model?
2) For streaming chunk cadence, do you prefer more frequent small chunks (~50ms) or slightly larger/batched chunks (~150-200ms)? This affects CPU and networking load.
3) Any constraints on connection types (SSE vs WebSocket)? We can support both; WebSocket gives lower overhead for many concurrent bi-directional streams.

Next steps I propose:
- I'll pull together a short SLO proposal and a perf runbook with recommended RT targets and batching/quantization knobs.
- Marissa will propose an initial runtime config for the patterns you described (TTFT optimization + streaming cadence).
- If that looks good, we can set up a short perf spike test in a dedicated environment (2-3 hours) to validate p95 TTFT and chunk cadence under your traffic shape.

Attaching a draft SLO proposal (redwood-ttft-proposal-acme.pdf) — please take a look and tell us which of the TTFT/throughput tradeoffs you want to prioritize.

If the items above look right, recommend we lock a perf test window next week (I’ll coordinate scheduling).

Thanks —
Aditya Rao

Hi Aditya —

Thanks for the clear recap — that matches how we see things. A couple quick clarifications from our side:
- TTFT target applies to our primary chat assistant model (and highest-priority user path). Lower-priority batch jobs can tolerate higher TTFT.
- Chunk cadence: we prefer ~75ms cadence for the live agent handoff experience. Important that the UI sees steady micro-chunks rather than occasional large bursts.
- Connection type: WebSocket is preferred across our web and mobile clients — we already use it for other live features.

One more operational note: during peak marketing events we expect long tail spikes (burst to 300 RPS for ~10 minutes) and we need predictable latency behavior during those windows. If you can show how Redwood would prioritize TTFT vs cost during bursts that'd help our procurement conversation.

Thanks —
Alyssa

Subject: Re: TTFT & streaming requirements — follow-up and proposed SLOs

Hi Alyssa / Tom —

Quick technical follow-up with how we'd approach meeting your constraints and the tradeoffs:

1) TTFT <= 150ms p95 (short prompts) — feasible with these levers:
   - Model placement: pin the primary model to dedicated GPU pools located in your primary region (us-west) to avoid cross-region network hops.
   - Short prompt path: compile an optimized fast-path for sequence lengths <=512 with attention kernel selection and reduced scheduling latency.
   - KV/prefix caching: for repeated context we keep warm KV caches to reduce token generation latency.

2) Streaming chunk cadence (~75ms preferred):
   - We can support ~50-100ms chunk cadence via our streaming runtime using WebSockets — note that smaller chunks increase CPU interrupts and network packets.
   - For 75ms we recommend chunk sizes ~8-16 tokens (model dependent) and keep batching window minimal for low latency.
   - If you want to trade a little user-perceived latency for cost, we can move to 120-150ms cadence with slightly larger chunks and better batching efficiency.

3) Throughput & spikes (80 RPS steady, 300 RPS burst):
   - Autoscale buffer: Dedicated pools with burst capacity to handle short spikes; we recommend a target headroom of 2.5x for the burst pattern you described.
   - Prioritization policy: we can configure traffic classes (primary chat = high priority). During capacity pressure, lower-priority routes can be deprioritized or redirected to quantized model variants.

4) Concurrency per session: 8 concurrent streams per user — within our runtime that maps to concurrent KV contexts; we need to size memory/slot allocations accordingly.

Perf validation plan (what we propose to test):
- Controlled perf run in dedicated environment: run mixed workload with your traffic shape (80 RPS steady, 300 RPS 10-minute spikes), measure p50/p95 TTFT, chunk cadence distribution, and per-token cost.
- We'll capture traces and provide middleware hooks so your SREs can replicate metrics in your stack.

I'll draft a config that maps to the SLOs Aditya attached and include expected cost deltas for the three cadence options (50ms, 75ms, 150ms).

Let me know if you want us to include a WebSocket sample client for your frontend team as part of the perf test.

—Marissa
